A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HARIS research. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated prompts and image-based case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original HARIS evaluations on EX-FEVER, HOVER and CHECKWHY, together with single-agent, coordination-round and reward ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds baseline comparisons, model-size experiments, supervised-fine-tuning results and human evaluation of the reward judge.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 corrects the returned agents from L_N and H_N to L_{N+1} and H_{N+1}, matching the final alternating update. This is a limited correction to the algorithm specification; the architecture, rollout actions, rewards and GRPO objective remain unchanged. It does not establish that the underlying experiments changed.

E1.justification: Both versions cover EX-FEVER with 2–3 hops, HOVER with 2–4 hops and positive CHECKWHY claims, using Wikipedia retrieval. The added comparisons and human checks reuse the existing claim-verification and synthesized-QA setting; they introduce no new domain or verification task.

E2.justification: v2 adds BiDeV to the main comparison in Table 1 and introduces supervised fine-tuning and ReAct comparisons in Tables 6 and 7. These substantially expand the evaluated alternatives. The original main-table comparators remain present.

E3.justification: v2 adds comparisons using Qwen3-4B across baselines, SFT with correct-answer-filtered training targets and matched epochs/learning rates, and ReAct evaluations at 4B, 8B and 14B. Appendix D introduces a human-validation protocol using 150 held-out questions and two annotators evaluating 75 responses each. These are additional protocols; the reported main evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 extends the reward ablation from training curves to final verification scores in Table 4. It also adds SFT-versus-RL comparisons, model-size sensitivity analysis and human validation of the reward judge in Appendices B and D. The earlier role-separation and coordination-round ablations and qualitative cases remain.

E5.justification: v2 introduces human–LLM agreement estimation, reporting Cohen’s kappa of 0.81 and 93.3% agreement. v1 contains no corresponding reliability statistics. Neither version reports benchmark seed-based variability, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Retained entries in Tables 1–3 and the original training curves are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results for BiDeV, reward choice, matched backbones, SFT, model scaling and human validation. For example, Table 4 reports HOVER 4-hop F1 of 52.38 with F1 rewards versus 57.42 with LLM-judge rewards. Table 5 shows FOLK tying HARIS on both EX-FEVER settings. These are additional comparisons, not improvements to the original HARIS scores.

T1.justification: The reward definitions and GRPO objective in Equations 1–4 are unchanged. No mathematical assumptions, theoretical results, proofs or substantive derivations are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims about coordinated reasoning/search and effective multi-hop verification. The introduction newly claims that HARIS is among the first RL-based cooperative-agent approaches for claim verification, adding a limited novelty claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning human alignment of the reward judge and the advantages of agent separation beyond simply increasing model size. Its limitations newly exclude open-domain QA and counterfactual detection. The original explanations concerning retrieval noise, agent coordination and binary-verification limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds a HARIS code-repository link and single-agent/SFT prompt templates in Table 9. It provides more specific GPU allocations, explicitly states one epoch per training stage, and documents SFT target generation and human-annotation instructions. Existing optimizer, retrieval and context-length details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Liu et al.’s BiDeV and explicitly contrasts HARIS’s cooperative RL training with prompt-based LoCal and BiDeV. The new early-work novelty claim sharpens this positioning, while the broader related-work coverage remains intact.

P1.justification: v2 edits and condenses passages throughout the introduction, methodology, ablations and case study, and clarifies the foundation and alternating training stages. It regroups appendices into settings, additional experiments, prompts/examples and human evaluation. The main section sequence and narrative remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds four result tables, a single-agent/SFT prompt table and a human-evaluation screenshot. It revises Figure 1’s labels/caption, expands the captions of Figures 8–9 and relocates existing tables. Figures 2–9 retain identical embedded images; v1’s prompt, signature and synthesis-example tables are preserved under new numbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical support by addressing backbone differences between methods, comparing RL with supervised training, testing model scaling, and validating the previously unchecked LLM reward against human judgments. Final reward-ablation scores also connect training behavior to verification performance. Appendix B.1 overstates uniform superiority—Table 5 shows FOLK ties on EX-FEVER—but this limited interpretive flaw does not outweigh the stronger controls and validation.
